newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn keeping payments to SS men secret, TV says.
newsitem.headline: Bonn keeping payments to SS men secret, TV says.

text.p: German government agencies are helping to conceal payments of disability pensions to members of Hitler's elite SS who live abroad, a television programme reported on Thursday.

NDR television's "Panorama" quoted the head of one pensions office as saying the practice was established because the veterans could expect reprisals from their neighbours or in some cases even treason charges if their past became public.
In a summary of a programme to be broadcast later on Thursday, Panorama highlighted SS veterans in Denmark.
It said the office responsible for the pensioners transferred the money via the German Red Cross to an association of expatriate Germans which then distributes the pensions.

A spokesman for the Labour Ministry, which is responsible for pensions, confirmed that it was legally possible to keep payments to former soldiers under wraps to protect them. He could not immediately comment on any specific cases.
A member of the opposition Greens Party, Volker Beck, vowed to raise the issue in parliament next week.
"The scale of this moral disaster is horrifying," Beck said. "The complicity of the pensions offices is a scandal."
The SS was an elite force notorious for its brutality during World War Two and its unswerving loyalty to Hitler.

Panorama reported last month that thousands of war criminals or members of army units which committed atrocities were receiving the so-called "victims' pensions", paid to anyone who suffers from a disability linked to World War Two.

Officials confirmed there was no provision in the law to exclude war criminals who lived in Germany, but that payments to those living abroad could be stopped if Bonn was made aware that they could be war criminals.

Beck called for the payment of supplementary pensions to all war criminals and anyone who had joined the SS voluntarily to be stopped. "The whole victims' pensions affair has already heavily damaged Germany's standing abroad," he said.
